rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage characterizes polytheism as attributing falsehood to God.
rows.anchor: ﷲimputing falsehood to God). The word رﺳﻞis used for angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The terms rasūl and malak share the same literal meaning, and the plural rasul can encompass the angel of death and his squad.
rows.anchor: purpose of using the plural رﺳﻞis to encompass angel of death and his squad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh will confess that all their supposed companions have been lost to them.
rows.anchor: The words “all of them have been lost upon us” signify the confession of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first phrase identifies companions as earlier jinn and human communities who followed Satan.
rows.anchor: They will be those before them from among the jinn and men who had followed Satan.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second phrase identifies Hell as their destination, so they have the worst companions and worst abode.
rows.anchor: The second expresses the place they will land in: Hell fire.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb darakū represents tadārakū, meaning that the earlier people caught up with those who came later.
rows.anchor: the preceding ones caught up with the later ones.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in the phrase about the earlier group indicates that the later group speaks about its predecessors.
rows.anchor: implying that the later ones will say about the previous ones.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍaʿf means “twice,” though contextual indications can make it refer to more.
rows.anchor: means “twice” and in the presence of concomitant indications can refer to more.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Former allies and leaders will turn on one another in Hell: followers curse their leaders, who blame and disown them.
rows.anchor: they will curse one another as soon as they will face each other.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Virtue and vice spread beyond their perpetrators across generations; even a small seed can grow into an immense legacy.
rows.anchor: both vice and virtue are contagious by their very nature.

rows.speaker: the Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to say that Cain, humanity’s first killer, receives a share of the sin of later unjust killings because he established the precedent.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws). In this narrative, he has stated the extent of the consequences of people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both earlier and later generations bear extra sin for their bad example; predecessors receive the requested double punishment, but successors also answer for influencing those after them.
rows.anchor: Besides their own sins, both the earlier and later generations will get another share of sins.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With istikbār, the preposition ʿan carries an implication explained earlier.
rows.anchor: In verse 40, the preposition used with

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closed-gates image means unbelievers will not receive the welcome granted to believers; they will be disgraced and driven toward Hell.
rows.anchor: the negation found in this sentence is not meant to negate the verb per se

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Classical Arabic uses comparable negation of an action’s consequence rather than the action itself.
rows.anchor: There are several examples of this usage in classical Arabic.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel-through-a-needle image is hyperbole for an impossibility, and the Gospels use a similar image in Matthew 19:23–24.
rows.anchor: are steeped in a special hyperbolic style. It means that it is impossible for such people to enter Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Gospel points to wealth as the cause of arrogance, while the Qur’an names arrogance itself as the real sin; the discussion recalls Adam and Satan.
rows.anchor: The only difference in the style of the Qur’ ān and the Bible is that Jesus (sws) has referred to the reason of arrogance which is wealth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account says that even a trace of arrogance bars a person from Paradise; Jesus’s “poor in spirit” saying is also cited.
rows.anchor: Earlier, in the episode of Adam (sws) and Satan, the essence of arrogance has been explained.

rows.speaker: Jesus (sws)
rows.claim: Jesus is reported to teach that the poor in spirit possess the kingdom of heaven.
rows.anchor: Jesus (sws) is also reported to have said: Blessed are the poor in spirit for theirs is the kingdom of heaven

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mahād means a spreading and ghawāshin is a plural form meaning covering; Hell covers its inhabitants above and below.
rows.anchor: The implication is that Hell will be their covering from above and below.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity is a parenthetical reassurance.
rows.anchor: form a parenthetical sentence and are meant for assurance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Banishment of grievance describes Paradise’s residents meeting with affection and welcome, with no malice between them.
rows.anchor: The style implied in “We shall banish every grievance of their hearts” needs to be appreciated.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Facing one another signifies love, whereas turning away signifies grievance; this affectionate scene parallels Hell’s mutual cursing.
rows.anchor: Sitting while facing away from each other signifies grievance and sitting while staring one another signifies love and affection.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s “forgetting” those who forgot the meeting means ignoring them, since God does not literally forget.
rows.anchor: they will be ignored by the Almighty; otherwise what is the meaning of God forgetting someone?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s promise to remember those who remember Him means favor, help, fulfillment of promises, and eternal blessing.
rows.anchor: He will look upon them with favour and help them at every instance; fulfil every promise made with them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The residents’ gratitude resembles a traveller’s thanksgiving after a long journey.
rows.anchor: depict the words of thanksgiving expressed by a traveller after a long journey.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “This” includes the truth-seeking urge and divine guidance delivered through messengers and prophets.
rows.anchor: to the urge seekers of the truth are blessed with but also to the guidance provided by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The perilous journey and unexpected success make the residents attribute their arrival to God’s blessing rather than their own effort.
rows.anchor: they will regard it to be purely a blessing of God; they will think not even think that it was their effort

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The residents declare the messengers truthful after seeing their reports come to pass, implicitly warning the deniers and arrogant people.
rows.anchor: is the proclamation made by the dwellers of Paradise after seeing every news given to them by messengers materialize.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although residents regard Paradise as God’s gift, God calls it the reward for their deeds; this completes His favor by letting them experience it as earned and personally theirs.
rows.anchor: This verse elevates the status of the deeds of people to such an extent that a higher status cannot be imagined.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Paradise an inheritance recalls Adam and Satan: only Adam’s descendants who keep faith and righteousness despite Satan’s lure become heirs, having won the contest.
rows.anchor: only those people from the progeny of Adam (sws) will become an heir to the Paradise of their forefather

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next passage has Paradise’s residents confirm that God’s promises were fulfilled; Hell’s residents agree, then a caller pronounces God’s curse on them.
rows.anchor: the dwellers of Paradise will inform the dwellers of Hell that all the promised God had made them have been fulfilled

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A group on the heights watches the outcomes in Heaven and Hell, recognizes people by their signs, congratulates Heaven’s residents, and curses Hell’s.
rows.anchor: a group of illustrious individuals will be made to observe what would ensue in Heaven and Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage recalls how arrogant factions trusted their power and swore the righteous could not enter Heaven, then asks where the mocked people and mockers ended.
rows.anchor: They will ask what benefit was their faction to them on which they do arrogantly relied.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell’s residents ask for water and Paradise’s residents refuse, citing God’s prohibition; the account is certain guidance that must be accepted before it is too late.
rows.anchor: At the end, a warning is sounded that the account of Heaven and Hell narrated is a certain fact.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Badr, Quraysh propaganda accused Muhammad of making his own tribe fight, killing or capturing them, demanding ransom, and plundering spoils to undermine the Prophet.
rows.anchor: how can he be a messenger of God when he is making people of the same tribe fight among themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before Badr, Quraysh invoked Muslim weakness as an excuse against Islam; after defeat, they shifted to accusations about the Prophet’s conduct.
rows.anchor: Before the battle took place, they presented the weakness and helplessness of the believers as an excuse against Islam.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an answers those objections and urges the Anṣār and Muhājirūn to preserve their brotherhood against the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: both should stand together as a solid wall against the disbelievers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–4 cite and briefly answer a question from weak Muslims, then call believers to fear God, repair resentments, obey, embody faith, and expect reward.
rows.anchor: An objection raised in the form of a question by some weak Muslims is cited and briefly responded to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims should faithfully obey God and His Messenger and not turn away from the Messenger in his presence.
rows.anchor: Muslims are directed to faithfully obey God and His Messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who are deaf and dumb and fail to think or understand are the worst creatures before God.
rows.anchor: The worst of animals before God are the deaf and the dumb who do not think and understand.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God found no ability in such people and therefore deprived them of the yearning to accept truth.
rows.anchor: God could not find any ability in them and for this reason deprived them of the yearning to accept the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims must not flee an organized attack; retreat brings God’s wrath and Hell.
rows.anchor: If they do so in the wake of an organized attack, they will earn the wrath of God and the punishment of Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When believers fight for God, He fights alongside them and grants opportunities to show their prowess, as at Badr, and will foil future disbeliever plans.
rows.anchor: God also fights with them and gives the believers the opportunities to show their prowess.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh are warned that their claimed test of truth has yielded a victory for the believers and that further mischief will meet God’s power; their large army cannot save them.
rows.anchor: They should see that victory has manifested itself.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims must obey the Messenger rather than resemble Jews who profess obedience but fail to practice it.
rows.anchor: This attitude is actually shown by the Jews: they would commit to obey but would in fact not do so.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who cannot hear or reason are the worst creatures; God found no capacity in them and withheld the desire to accept truth, which He grants to receptive people.
rows.anchor: Only those people are blessed with this urge from God who have the ability to be influenced and accept the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Messenger’s preaching gives life to the heart and soul; hesitation can meet God’s practice that separates a person from the ability to choose good.
rows.anchor: the preaching of God’s Messenger is life for their heart and soul.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In communal life, failure to reform some people’s wrongs makes everyone bear their consequences; Muslims should trust God to help Islam as He did when they were few.
rows.anchor: if people do not try to reform the mistakes made by some specific individuals, then every person good or bad, has to bear their evil consequences.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers must honor their pledge; love of wealth and children is a trial that should not displace love of God and His Messenger, and those who resist worldly entanglement receive discernment and forgiveness.
rows.anchor: The love for wealth and children should not hinder them to fulfil the requisites of love for God and His Messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is reminded that God repeatedly helped believers and frustrated Quraysh’s plans; the Quraysh called the Qur’an ancient tales and demanded stones or punishment as proof.
rows.anchor: They demanded that if Muḥammad is God’s Messenger, they will only believe in him if stones be hurled

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh claimed stewardship of the Kaʿbah but lacked knowledge of its history and purpose; only God-fearing people deserve that role, and clapping and whistling are no Abrahamic prayer.
rows.anchor: Clapping hands and whistling are regarded by them to be their prayer.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh’s spending to block God’s path and defeat Islam is futile and will become a source of regret.
rows.anchor: All their spending will become a means of regret for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gathers the evil elements together and consigns them to Hell.
rows.anchor: God will gather all these evil elements and consign them to Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh can have past wrongs forgiven by reforming; if they persist, they will share earlier rejecters’ fate, while believers fight until persecution ends and God’s religion alone prevails.
rows.anchor: they will meet the same fate as the one met by the rejecters of the previous prophets.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening question about spoils is answered: contentment with God’s and the Messenger’s distribution signifies true faith, and Badr’s meeting was God’s design to distinguish truth from falsehood and establish clear proof.
rows.anchor: He wanted a decisive battle to be fought between the believers and the Quraysh so that truth and falsehood become evident as a result.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made the enemy look small in the Prophet’s dream and both armies seem small to one another, giving each courage to fight and making the decisive encounter possible.
rows.anchor: the army of the disbelievers was made to appear trivial by God in the eyes of the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Badr proves God decisively helped the believers; future success requires strength, courage, remembrance, obedience without dispute, and perseverance, for God is with the steadfast.
rows.anchor: They must fully obey God and His Messenger and not differ in any matter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims must not imitate the disbelievers’ arrogant battlefield display; Satan promised invincibility and companionship but fled in fear of God, a subtle sarcasm on Jews.
rows.anchor: when he saw the battlefield, he became scared and ran away, right in accordance with his tradition.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hypocrites and envious people belittled Muslims’ confidence, not realizing that God’s power and wisdom support them.
rows.anchor: These hypocrites did not know that great is God’s trust.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Badr begins Quraysh’s humiliation; their fate is the natural result of their own deeds, like Pharaoh’s people, whom God warned and then destroyed after further rebellion.
rows.anchor: God does not change His attitude with a nation until that nation changes its own attitude.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet must deal firmly with treaty-breakers so their supporters are shaken, strengthen defenses against known and hidden enemies, accept peace proposals in trust, and rely on God against deception.
rows.anchor: If in the garb of peace they want to deceive the Prophet (sws), sufficient for them is the God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God fully compensates believers for whatever they spend in military preparation.
rows.anchor: Whatever the believers spend in this cause will be fully compensated before God and no reduction would come about.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God suffices the Prophet despite few followers; he should urge them to fight, since faith and resolve let twenty brave believers face two hundred and a hundred face a thousand.
rows.anchor: Twenty of his brave warriors are sufficient for two hundred warriors of the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revealed later as Muslims multiplied, this verse lowers the ratio to one believer for two disbelievers because later Muslims had less faith than the earliest.
rows.anchor: The reason for this reduction was that these later Muslims did not have the same extent of faith as that of the early Muslims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh accused the Prophet of killing and ransoming his own people for political power; the Qur’an blames their worldly desire, says prophets do not seek it, and permits spoils to believers.
rows.anchor: Now they started to say that Muḥ ammad (sws), God forbid, was desirous of political authority

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every nation has a fixed respite, so the Quraysh received warning instead of immediate destruction.
rows.anchor: God has prescribed a certain period of respite for every nation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Badr’s captives are told that sincere hearts and gratitude for release can open new paths, but renewed treachery will bring another Muslim victory like Badr.
rows.anchor: if God found good in their hearts and if they valued the favour that they were released after ransom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage institutes brotherhood between the Muhājirūn and Anṣār.
rows.anchor: Brotherhood is instituted between the muhājirūn and the anṣār.
